articles.title: Key takeaways from the 2026 midterm elections in California
articles.summary: Democrats easily hold on to governor’s office and are on track to notch up wins in key congressional races.
articles.body:
While votes are still being counted in California, a handful of important races in the midterm elections have already been called or are pointing firmly in one direction.

Despite its status as a reliably Democratic stronghold, the Western state has played a dynamic role in Tuesday’s United States elections, acting as a testing ground for questions as varied as partisan redistricting and tax measures targeting billionaires.

Let’s take a quick look at some of tonight’s results:

While vote-counting was still under way, Democratic candidates have pulled decisively ahead in several contests seen as must-wins for the party’s effort to take control of the US House of Representatives.

To boost the party’s chances, voters a year ago approved a partisan redistricting measure promoted by Governor Gavin Newsom to net Democrats five additional seats in the US House.

One such race took place in the state’s 22nd Congressional District , located in the agriculture-rich Central Valley.

Progressive educator Randy Villegas celebrated the results of the race on Tuesday night as the Democrat held a commanding lead of about 30 percentage points over Republican incumbent David Valadao.

Democratic candidate Marni von Wilpert is also ahead in the 48th district, located in Southern California near San Diego, where she is leading Republican Jim Desmond by about 20 points.

While those advantages are considerable, The Associated Press news agency has not yet officially called those races.

Progressive Aisha Wahab is also firmly ahead in her race against Melissa Hernandez, a fellow Democrat, in the 14th district.

Wahab overcame substantial spending by pro-Israel groups to defeat the establishment-aligned Hernandez in a special election in September. She is now on track to win a full term in that seat.

With her previous victory, Wahab became the first person of Afghan ancestry elected to Congress.

In the San Francisco Bay Area, moderate Democrat Scott Wiener is leading progressive rival Connie Chan in a race for the seat of retiring Representative Nancy Pelosi, the powerful former Democratic House speaker. Wiener has a lead of about 10 points with 50 percent of the vote tallied thus far.

Republicans face another bruising defeat in gubernatorial race

While Republicans across the country have laboured to turn California into a symbol of liberal dysfunction, voters in the state remain unconvinced that conservatives offer a better alternative.

The gubernatorial race was called for the Democratic candidate, former state Attorney General Xavier Becerra, immediately after the polls closed.

Becerra’s Republican rival, British political commentator Steve Hilton, had argued that years of unbroken Democratic domination had resulted in sky-high prices and public disorder.

But his bid to underscore cost-of-living issues by holding campaign events where he offered discounted petrol fell flat at a time when many voters blame President Donald Trump’s war on Iran for eye-watering prices at the pump.

Becerra’s victory comes more than five years after Republicans tried to dislodge Newsom through a recall election that failed by a margin of more than 20 points.

In the past, Republicans could console themselves that if they remained in electoral purgatory in the most populous US state, their Democratic rivals were likewise locked out of power in conservative strongholds such as Texas.

Tuesday’s losses will sting a bit more after a series of shock wins by Democrats in states that can usually be counted on to deliver easy wins for Republicans, including Texas.

While some results have come in quickly, tight contests over some of the state’s ballot measures, or policy questions put directly before voters, have yet to be called.

Proposition 40, which would institute a one-time tax on the net worth of billionaires in the state to help fund programmes such as healthcare and education, is trailing with about 44 percent of the counted votes in favour and 56 percent against.

The measure won support from progressive figures, such as Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Ro Khanna, but prompted a deluge of spending from wealthy donors and companies to oppose it.

The Associated Press has announced that Proposition 39, which would have instituted voter ID laws sought by conservatives, has been rejected by voters.

articles.title: Good news for Agniveers: Government extends tenure by two years
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet on Wednesday announced a two-year extension of the engagement period for Agniveers enrolled in the Army under the 'Agnipath'
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet on Wednesday announced a two-year extension of the engagement period for Agniveers enrolled in the Army under the 'Agnipath' scheme.During a press conference, Chief of Defence Staff (CDS) General NS Raja Subramani said that the 75 percent of the first batch of Agniveers who were earlier set to exit after four years will now be offered an option to apply for enrolment in the armed forces. Their enrolment will be subject to selection criteria."Today is a very significant day for the Indian Defence Forces and for our 'Agniveers'. The Cabinet has created a pathway for all Agniveers to be absorbed into the Indian Army. As you are aware, the 'Agnipath' scheme was introduced on June 14, 2022. At that time, it was stated that there would be continuous performance evaluation of the Agniveers and that the scheme would be reviewed periodically. The first batch of Agniveers is now nearing the completion of their four-year tenure. Based on the performance evaluations conducted over these four years, we have received very positive feedback regarding their performance. As you know, 25% of the Agniveers are to be enrolled into the regular forces based on merit," the CDS said."Previously, the provision was for 75% of the Agniveers to transition back into society as disciplined and motivated youth. However, under this updated scheme, the remaining 75% of Agniveers will now be offered an additional engagement period of two years," he added."Upon completion of this two-year period, all those who are willing will be enrolled into the armed forces, subject to objective selection criteria. These are the four major aspects of this scheme. After the two years, they will be given an option to get absorbed, subject to their willingness and an objective selection process," he further said.Defence minister Rajnath Singh thanked Prime Minister Narendra Modi and said that the decision is continuation of long-term structural reforms of the defence forces."Taking a significant decision today, the Union Cabinet chaired by PM Shri Narendra Modi has approved a two-year ‘Second Tour of Duty’ for Agniveers under Agnipath. I sincerely thank PM Modi for taking the decision of additional 2-year ‘Second Tour of Duty’ for Agniveers under the Agnipath scheme. This would also provide enrollment of all willing Agniveers as regular soldiers after the tenure of 4/6 years, who meet the selection criteria," Rajnath Singh said in a social media post on X."This decision is continuation of long-term structural reforms of our defence forces, aimed at creating a younger, fitter, technologically equipped and future-ready military. It is not merely a recruitment policy; it is a way forward to prepare India's military for the changing character of warfare," he added.The Agnipath scheme was introduced by the Union Cabinet in 2022 to recruit Agniveers into the armed forces under the respective Service Acts for a period of four years.The decision comes amid criticism of the shorter engagement period, which prompted several states, including Uttar Pradesh, Haryana and Maharashtra, to provide reservations for Agniveers in police and other services.The scheme was introduced to provide young people with an opportunity to serve the country and contribute to nation-building, while making the armed forces' profile youthful and dynamic.

articles.title: GOP’s redistricting gamble backfires in Florida as Democrats hold ground
articles.summary: Trump’s party dealt a setback as Republican bid to tilt Florida’s House map falters on a strong night for Democrats.
articles.body:
The Democratic Party has won several United States House of Representatives seats that Florida’s Republican-led legislature redrew to favour the GOP in a redistricting effort.

In a sweeping result reflecting Democrats’ broader midterm election victory , Kathy Castor held Florida’s 14th congressional district, which swung nearly 16 percentage points towards Democrats compared with its 2024 presidential vote.

Democratic first-time candidate Pia Dandiya won the 22nd district, and Jared Moskowitz retained the 25th.

Notably, the race between incumbent Darren Soto and Republican challenger Dan Green in Florida’s 9th district remained the closest of the four, with Soto holding a slim lead as the final votes were counted on Wednesday .

The wins add to a wave of Democratic victories across the nation, in an election widely cast as a referendum on President Donald Trump. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, including at least 54 Senate seats, a major setback for Trump that could provide a significant check on his power in his final two years in office.

Florida’s returns also offer another measure of the electoral headwinds facing Republicans this election cycle, despite tilting the district map in their favour to make several seats more Republican-friendly.

Longtime Trump ally and outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis and the state’s Republican-controlled legislature redrew Florida’s congressional map in April, seeking to bolster the party’s chances of retaining control of the US House.

The move formed part of an unprecedented nationwide Republican effort to secure a structural advantage ahead of the midterms by reshaping the boundaries of congressional representation.

The revised boundaries gave Trump’s party a lead in four Democratic-held districts: the 9th, 14th, 22nd, and 25th, and were explicitly engineered to compress the state’s Democratic delegation in the US House.

Under the new map, signed into law by DeSantis in May, Trump would have carried three of the four districts by double-digit margins during his 2024 presidential campaign, and the fourth by roughly 9 percentage points.

At the time, some had argued that redrawing the map may backfire on Republicans, diluting the party’s strongholds and tightening margins at a time when Trump’s approval ratings had dipped to an all-time low amid the economic knock-ons of the US-Israel war on Iran.

Redistricting is the process of redrawing electoral boundaries, usually after the US census every 10 years, to account for population shifts and ensure districts maintain roughly equal populations.

The boundaries determine which voters are grouped together to elect a representative to the US House.

Because the party in power in a state legislature often has a hand in drawing the map, the process can be used to give one party an electoral advantage – a practice known as gerrymandering.

Following tit-for-tat map re-drawings, Republicans hoped to net at least 13 seats nationally, though polling had suggested their gains may be much more muted.

articles.title: Syrians see Israel as biggest regional threat, followed by Iran: Survey
articles.summary: Some 97% of respondents to Arab Opinion Index for Syria say Israel threatens security and stability in the Middle East.
articles.body:
Most Syrians view Israel as the greatest threat to the security of their country and the region, with Iran a distant second, according to a new nationwide survey.

The poll, conducted by the Doha-based Arab Center for Research and Policy Studies and the Arab Center for Contemporary Syria Studies, published its results on Monday.

The Arab Opinion Index for Syria 2026 found that 61 percent of respondents named Israel as the main threat to Syria, while Iran was named by 20 percent, Turkiye by 6 percent and the United States by 5 percent.

Asked about the Arab world as a whole, 58 percent of respondents named Israel as the main threat, unchanged from last year. Meanwhile, the share naming Iran as the main regional threat doubled from 12 percent in 2025 to 24 percent.

Some 97 percent said Israel threatens the security and stability of the Middle East, up from 78 percent a year earlier. The percentage of those who said the same about Iran rose from 74 to 93.

Israel has seized territory in southern Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024. About 96 percent of respondents said Israel is working to destabilise Syria and 86 percent said it is driving separatist tendencies.

Almost 80 percent oppose recognising Israel, up from 74 percent in 2025, and 74 percent oppose any agreement that does not return the occupied Golan Heights. Respondents were split on direct talks between Syrian and Israeli officials: 41 percent said they serve Syria’s interests and 49 percent said they do not.

Al Jazeera interviewed residents on the streets of Damascus ahead of the Israeli elections last month. One of them, Jihad el-Hamwi, said Israel’s approach to Syria was unaffected by the change of government.

“In my opinion, Israeli policy does not change when the ruler changes, because it is an expansionist policy,” he said. “Just as it has expanded into Syria, Palestine, Lebanon and other countries, its aim is expansion, not a change of ruler.”

Another resident told Al Jazeera, “The Israeli elections only ever bring in a ruler who is unjust, who does not even recognise the rights of his neighbours, and who has absolutely no connection to international norms.”

On the US-Israel war on Iran, 80 percent of survey respondents said Iranian missile strikes on Israel were justified, with 74 percent saying Iranian strikes on Arab countries, other than US military bases, were not. Three-quarters said Washington had waged the war on Israel’s behalf.

The survey also points to growing support for pluralism: 76 percent agreed that democracy, despite its problems, is better than other systems, up 16 percentage points from last year. Three-quarters said a democratic system with political pluralism and a separation of powers was best for Syria. No alternative, including rule by Islamic law without elections, drew more than 9 percent.

About 87 percent of respondents said no one should question the patriotism of people who oppose government policy, a 20-point increase.

Views of the country’s direction were mixed. Half said Syria was heading the right way, citing the end of the former government, the release of detainees and the lifting of sanctions, but 35 percent disagreed.

The survey comes nearly two years after al-Assad was toppled in an offensive led by opposition fighters, ending more than five decades of his family’s rule.

articles.title: Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins in Michigan to become first Muslim senator
articles.summary: El-Sayed bested Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator in US history.
articles.body:
Left-wing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has won in the battleground state of Michigan to become the US's first Muslim senator, following a race fuelled by withering attacks and inter-party disputes.

El-Sayed bested Republican Mike Rogers, withstanding an onslaught of attacks that included baselessly tying him to terrorism and a high-profile spat with a fellow Democrat.

Rogers, backed by President Donald Trump, portrayed El-Sayed as a communist, criticising his stance on Israel and his Muslim faith.

After waiting long hours, watching the wave of Democratic gains across the country, El-Sayed's supporters celebrated wildly when he took the stage to mark his victory.

The former public health administrator campaigned on a left-wing platform that included universal health care and a wealth tax on billionaires.

The win comes days after El-Sayed's Democratic primary rival, Haley Stevens, endorsed Rogers, the Republican candidate, just days before the election.

El-Sayed's supporters gave deafening cheers when he took to the stage, as they chanted his name in jubilation. A sea of iPhones were held up to take in this moment of history - a Muslim man elected to the Senate.

Several people in the crowd embraced, filled with emotion. They repeated his slogan back to him like they were at a concert: "Money out of politics, money in your pocket and Medicare for all."

On the campaign trail, El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, described Israel's actions in Gaza as genocide and called for an end to US aid to the country.

The issue carries particular resonance in Michigan, which is home to the second largest Arab-American population in the US.

It also fuelled tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, whose primary campaign received millions of dollars in backing from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac).

The contest was widely seen as a test of the political influence of the Democratic left in a key battleground state, following a series of primary wins by democratic socialist candidates in more politically favoured districts.

El-Sayed thanked the crowd in the early hours of Wednesday morning for taking a chance on "the unlikeliest of candidates" and rounded on his opponents.

"They went all in on one of the ugliest campaigns we've seen in a long time," he said, accusing them of attacking him "because of my name and my faith".

"They wanted an America that is too small for some of us. We know that this is an America that is big enough for all of us," El-Sayed added.

This is a milestone for Muslim Americans who had to watch, along with their children, as El-Sayed was attacked with increasing anti-Muslim rhetoric, including directly from the president of the United States. It comes at a time of rising in Islamophobia nationwide.

Roula Allouch, an Arab American Muslim, told the BBC she had goosebumps from the success of the campaign.

"I'm proud of Abdul, the campaign that he ran, his family for their perseverance through all the hate, the Islamophobic rhetoric that was thrown at him throughout this campaign," she said.

Another Muslim woman in the crowd was equally moved and told the BBC his win meant everything to her.

"He makes us so proud and it just makes us feel like we can stand a little taller, broaden our shoulders and know somebody has our back and that he's going to be in Washington really fighting for us," she said.

El-Sayed has certainly shown on the campaign trail that he's willing to hit back at Maga attacks. In his victory speech, he used the Arabic phrase "Alhamdullah", and then trolled Republicans by saying that "for the rightwing ops, that just means praise be to God".

El-Sayed, 42, represents a generation of Arab Americans and Muslims who were born in the United States to immigrant parents and grew up in post-9/11 America.

Celebrating with family from Chicago, another South Asian Muslim supporter of El-Sayed's said the moment was historic for everyone who has been made to feel that they don't belong in America or have a place in politics.

"If someone with the name of Abdul can make it, that means this next generation can look up and say that they can too," she told the BBC.

The Michigan Senate seat, previously held by retiring Democrat Gary Peters, was considered by analysts to be one of the tightest races in Tuesday's midterm elections.

El-Sayed's win further cements Democrats' control of the US Senate after a wave of wins - including in deep-Republican areas.

He had to contend with massive outside spending heavily favouring Rogers and his opponent in the Democratic primary, Haley Stevens. He's been unapologetic and unwavering in his stances.

In presidential elections, Michigan is one of the crucial swing states - the state voted for Joe Biden in 2020 but Donald Trump in 2024.

Many had questioned whether Stevens' last-minute endorsement of Rogers would make a difference in the race.

Democratic leadership called it "a despicable betrayal" and her staff reportedly resigned in mass. Voters who spoke with the BBC in the state said they were confused over the move, with some questioning whether the congresswoman was acting out of anger.

El-Sayed attempted to ignore the dramatic turn, telling reporters that he doesn't "think about Haley Stevens" and "none of this matters".

Throughout his campaign, El-Sayed has channelled grassroots frustration with Washington politics as well as US ties to Israel. He took on money in politics and argued against Trump's policies, which he blamed for raising costs for voters in the state.

He campaigned with left-wing leaders Sen Bernie Sanders and Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

articles.body: World leaders have reacted to the outcome of the US midterm elections, with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa saying the results would introduce a “new era in world relations”, while Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez described the Republican defeats as a setback for the far-right. Iran’s chief negotiator with the United States, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said American voters had rejected war and warned Washington against going against public opinion.Ramaphosa, speaking to reporters on Wednesday, said the Democratic Party’s victories in both chambers of Congress reflected the will of the American people."We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken," he said.Sanchez also commented on the results, saying American voters had rejected policies that “only impoverish”, as well as hate, sexism and climate change denialism.In a post on X, the Spanish prime minister said, "Yesterday, American society voted against the policies that only impoverish. Against hate. Against machismo. Against climate denialism and against the privileges of the elites. It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will happen soon in Spain."He added that the far-right wave was losing momentum, saying, "The ultra wave that Feijóo and Abascal are trying to ride is no longer growing: it is crumbling."Ghalibaf, meanwhile, linked the Republican losses to public opposition to the war with Iran. His remarks came after US President Donald Trump acknowledged that the conflict had contributed to his party's poor performance in the midterm elections."Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Ghalibaf said in a post on X."If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," he added.The reactions followed a major Democratic victory in Tuesday's midterm elections, with the party winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The results are set to usher in a period of congressional resistance to Trump's administration.The elections reflected voter frustration over high prices, the war with Iran and concerns about government corruption. Democrats made gains across the country, flipping seats in states that had voted Republican for decades and that Trump had won by double-digit margins in the 2024 presidential election.Among the notable victories was James Talarico's Senate win in Texas, where no Democrat had won a statewide office in more than 30 years. Annie Andrews also defeated Republican Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina. Trump had backed the losing candidates in both races.In Michigan, progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers. Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine also lost her re-election bid to Democrat Troy Jackson.The results pointed to a shift among sections of the coalition that had helped Trump return to the White House two years ago. According to the AP Voter Poll, younger voters and Latino voters moved away from Republicans. About one-third of Hispanic voters said they had backed the Republican candidate in their local US House races.The outcome marked a setback for Trump, who spent much of the final month of the campaign holding rallies to mobilise Republican supporters but was unable to prevent significant losses for his party.You use AI every day. articles.title: Why Texas turning Blue is Elon Musk’s ‘biggest defeat’
articles.summary: Some of the richest people in American politics spent heavily backing Republicans in November 3 elections but their side lost the Senate’s control.
articles.body: Some of the richest people in American politics spent heavily backing Republicans in November 3 elections but their side lost the Senate’s control. Nowhere did it sting more than in Texas where Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton for the Senate, even though Elon Musk spent a fortune to help Paxton, according to a New York Times analysis. Democrat Gina Hinojosa also won the governor’s race. For a state that has anchored the Republican map for over 30 years, it is a stunning turn. For Musk, who donated a total $474 million (nearly half a billion dollars) to Republican candidates, including more than $220 million in Texas alone in this year’s midterm elections, it is arguably his biggest political defeat.How much Tesla CEO put in and why Texas matters to Elon MuskMusk was the largest donor of the 2026 midterms. Most of it went to his own America PAC and to the top super PACs for Senate and House Republicans. His biggest play was in Texas, his adopted home state and the headquarters of Tesla and SpaceX. In September alone, he gave $158 million to the Senate Republicans’ main super PAC, which was quickly routed to a super PAC backing Paxton, the state’s attorney general. America PAC also spent more than $47 million against Talarico. The New York Times put Musk’s total spending in the state at roughly $224 million.His reasoning was the long game. Musk has said Republicans needed a defence in case Democrats sweep Washington in 2028, and he feared they would grant statehood to Washington, DC and Puerto Rico. In a post on X on October 30, Musk gave a “game over” warning “for America”.My biggest concern is that if there is a clean sweep by Democrats of the House, Senate and Presidency in 2028, they will:1. Make DC and Puerto Rico states to gain a strong majority in the Senate.2. Open the borders and legalize everyone living in America illegally to cement a permanent majority.3. Increase the size of the Supreme Court to gain an immediate majority.This would result in America becoming a permanent one-party state and the end of democracy in any meaningful sense of the word.All that is needed to ensure this doesn’t happen is 51 Republican senators in 2029. That is why you should vote for Republican senators this election. Other reasons are irrelevant compared to this one.It would be game over for AmericaTexas is home turf for Musk and the tech worldTexas, with its cowboy hats, slow-smoked barbecue, favorable tax policies and fewer regulations, was supposed to be the antidote to California for tech people purportedly fed up with Silicon Valley’s Democratic politics. Other reasons Musk promoted Texas over California are relatively low-cost real estate and housing, and business-friendly environment.Musk helped build that image. He moved Tesla’s headquarters to Texas in 2021. In 2024, he moved SpaceX’s incorporation there from Delaware, after a Delaware judge invalidated his $56 billion Tesla pay plan. Musk said: “SpaceX has moved its state of incorporation from Delaware to Texas! If your company is still incorporated in Delaware, I recommend moving to another state as soon as possible.”He has also said SpaceX’s main office would move to Boca Chica and X would move to Austin. Many tech moguls came to Texas looking for redder politics. On Tuesday, the state turned a lot bluer.What Musk said after the resultElon Musk responded on X with jokes.“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he wrote, and then, “Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time.”Later he reposted conservative exit polling that showed Republican voters still backing the Trump administration’s immigration policies but seeing the war in Iran as a “losing issue.” His reply was one word: “Interesting.”The jokes follow a sharper tone in October, when he wrote, “Live by the sword, die by the sword,” and warned that he would find out who is “really pulling the strings.” An October report by Politico said that democrats are eyeing many targets, the biggest of them may be Elon Musk, as they make plans to probe corruption in and around President Donald Trump’s administration if they win control of the House next month.Musk’s influence on US electionsMusk’s returns have been uneven. In 2024 he spent over $290 million, mostly to help Donald Trump retake the White House, and later became the effective head of the DOGE office. In 2025 he and allied super PACs spent over $20 million on a Wisconsin Supreme Court race, and his favoured candidate lost by more than 10 points. With Texas now ‘Blue’, next up are the 2028 presidential primaries.A bad night for big moneyMusk was not the only billionaire to come up short. In Ohio, Vivek Ramaswamy lost the governor’s race to Democrat Amy Acton after putting an estimated $36 million of his own money into it. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms beat Republican billionaire Rick Jackson. In Texas, Governor Greg Abbott, who began the year with $105.7 million on hand, conceded to Hinojosa. According to the Associated Press, Democrats also won both the House and the Senate. Whether or not Texas is truly a battleground now, Republicans can no longer take its voters for granted.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Zelenskyy honours US First Lady Melania Trump for helping secure ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded US First Lady Melania Trump a state honour for her role in helping organise a humanitarian evacuation
articles.body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has awarded US First Lady Melania Trump a state honour for her role in helping organise a humanitarian evacuation from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky last week, according to a presidential decree published on Wednesday.The decree, dated November 2, cited her “significant personal contribution” to humanitarian support for Ukraine and her efforts to help Ukrainian children, including those deported or forcibly transferred from Russian-occupied territories.Melania Trump has been awarded the Order of Princess Olga, First Class. The distinction is given to women for exceptional contributions in areas including science, education, culture and charitable work, Reuters reported.Ukrainian officials have credited the US first lady with playing a pivotal role in arranging a six-day ceasefire that allowed civilians to be evacuated from Oleshky in southern Ukraine.The local truce ended on Sunday and was the longest pause in fighting in a specific area since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.Melania Trump said nearly 800 people had been evacuated during the operation.Melania Trump to host Russian, Ukrainian representatives at White HouseThe award follows the humanitarian operation in Oleshky, which allowed emergency supplies to reach residents and enabled civilians to leave the Russian-occupied town.The US first lady had described the ceasefire as a step towards lasting peace. In a post on X on Sunday, she said the truce across Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region had given residents access to food, clean water and medicine, while allowing them to move without the constant threat of attack.“Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace,” she wrote.The White House had announced on Tuesday that Melania Trump would host representatives from Russia and Ukraine on Thursday to discuss the ceasefire and the humanitarian operation.She was scheduled to deliver remarks on the initiative at 11 am EST.A Ukrainian official told The Kyiv Independent that Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and Russia's human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova were expected to attend.Evacuation from Russian-occupied OleshkyZelenskyy confirmed on Saturday that a humanitarian operation had taken place in Oleshky. He said a ceasefire had been established in the Kherson sector, roads leading to the town had been cleared of mines and humanitarian aid had been delivered.He also said people requiring evacuation had been moved out of the town and surrounding community. Ukrainian citizens from Oleshky had crossed into Ukrainian-controlled territory through the border in the Chernihiv region and would receive the necessary assistance.Melania Trump's role in the operation was described by the White House as an independently pursued initiative, with the first lady engaging with both countries to secure the local ceasefire.However, a Le Monde report claimed the humanitarian operation had been negotiated over four months by Russia's GRU and Ukraine's HUR military intelligence agencies.Citing sources, the French newspaper reported that the two sides had agreed to credit Melania Trump with the ceasefire to appease US President Donald Trump as he sought progress in peace negotiations.Oleshky has remained under Russian occupation since 2022. Residents had faced shortages of food, drinking water, electricity and medical supplies, while humanitarian organisations had been unable to deliver aid.The Kremlin has publicly ruled out further humanitarian operations of this kind in the foreseeable future.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘I will not delete my posts’: Inside Uganda’s crackdown on online critics
articles.summary: Uganda’s online critics allege abductions and intimidation as families search for missing relatives.
articles.body:
Kampala, Uganda – Praise Aloikin Opoloje walks into the visitors’ waiting room at Luzira Women’s Prison wearing an oversized yellow-and-black striped dress and a broad smile.

Detained since September 26, 2026, she was charged with the alleged unlawful use of a SIM card registered in her mother’s name. Her case has drawn attention to the risks faced by Ugandans who use social media to criticise powerful political and military figures.

Opoloje appeared before the Buganda Road Chief Magistrate’s Court on September 28, charged with using another person’s SIM card to carry out illegal activity.

She denied the charge under Regulation 29 of Uganda’s 2024 Regulation of Interception of Communications Regulations.

Opoloje says her detention followed a video in which she declared that she was not afraid of General Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Uganda’s military chief and son of President Yoweri Museveni.

A video, an arrest and an alleged threat

Opoloje says she was lured to a Kampala police station by a false accusation that she had stolen a carpet. She alleges that six men then forced her into a Toyota HiAce van, locally known as a “drone”.

“We are going to show you what we do to people who insult our president,” one of the men allegedly told her.

She says the men beat her, threatened to rape her and drove towards Entebbe. She feared they were taking her somewhere she might be tortured. According to Opoloje, a phone call prompted the men to turn back towards Kampala Central Police Station.

Her account of the alleged abduction and mistreatment could not be independently verified.

Asked whether she would cease speaking out, Opoloje said, “Me? Never. In fact, when I get out, if I do, I will start from where I stopped. I cannot keep quiet seeing what is going on in the country.”

Opoloje says she feared being taken to a basement where, she believes, people are tortured and raped. “Being in here in prison is better than being in the basement that they were taking me to,” she says.

Since Al Jazeera’s interview with her, Opoloje was granted bail on October 14, with court permission required before travelling internationally.

She also alleges that men have threatened her mother, telling her they knew where she lived. Opoloje says her detention has affected her family, including her three-year-old daughter.

“I don’t think my mother or my three-year-old daughter should pay the price for my actions,” she says.

For Emmanuel Baliza, 59, the uncertainty is different: he says he does not know where his 17-year-old son, William, is being held.

Emmanuel says armed men took William from their home after the teenager expressed an intention to protest against police brutality and Uganda’s education system.

According to Emmanuel, a stranger first lured him away using a pretext involving land. He says about six men wearing military uniforms and face coverings were waiting in a Toyota HiAce van and searched his phone.

“I told them, that’s my son, 17-year-old William Baliza,” Emmanuel says.

He alleges that the men took William, claiming they were arresting him for planning to protest after the elections. They reportedly told Emmanuel they were taking his son to the Special Investigations Unit, which handles serious and high-profile crimes, but did not provide a reference number.

Emmanuel says he later heard that William might be held at a military detention facility in Kasenyi near Entebbe. He says officials denied holding his son, leaving the family without confirmation of his whereabouts.

According to Emmanuel, his daughter told him William had posted a message on TikTok reading: “Uganda is bleeding.”

Reporting on the powerful, facing the consequences

Journalist and human rights activist Andrew Tabandama Natumanya says his reporting on a security operation involving properties linked to former Parliament Speaker Anita Among brought scrutiny from security personnel.

In May, officers searched properties linked to Among amid investigations into allegations including corruption and money laundering. Media reports said luxury vehicles, including a 2025 Rolls-Royce Cullinan, were seized.

Andrew says he posted real-time updates about the operation on X, formerly Twitter. He believes the attention his reporting attracted stemmed partly from questions about how he obtained information from within security agencies.

“Their main discomfort was, ‘How is he getting this information? How is he aware of what is happening at the Criminal Investigations Department? Who is giving me these updates?’” he says.

Andrew alleges that on June 17, 2026, a stranger lured him to a washing bay, where armed personnel forced him into a van.

He says he was taken away, assaulted and humiliated. According to Andrew, officers placed his head beneath one officer’s feet before stripping him naked and photographing him.

“Not even a pair of socks was on my body,” he says.

He further alleges that officers warned him against continuing to publish his updates online.

“You keep posting what you post, you will also see these things on the internet,” he recalls them saying.

Andrew says he was detained for five days before being released on bail. He also alleges that the experience had consequences for his family, including threats and difficulties affecting their businesses and employment prospects.

“Some of them are slowly but surely turning into unemployable citizens, and some of their businesses are being crippled down,” he says.

Despite what he describes as intimidation, Andrew says he will continue reporting.

“I will not delete my (posts). I will change tactics, but continue stating facts.”

“We want to see a free Uganda,” he adds.

Among was placed under house arrest, but was later ordered released by President Yoweri Museveni, and the state decided not to pursue charges.

Andrew’s account of abuse and harassment has not been independently verified.

When online speech becomes a legal battle

Steven Atukwatse, a lawyer with the Agora Research Center, a human rights organisation, says he has represented social media users charged under Uganda’s Computer Misuse Act, many of them TikTok and X users.

“Most are arrested for either criticising Museveni or his son, Muhoozi,” he says.

Atukwatse says he personally has handled 12 such cases since November 2025.

He describes cases in which families struggle to establish where relatives are being held.

“They disappear, then a few months later they are dumped at police stations,” he says.

When families ask authorities about missing relatives, he says, they are often told: “We do not have the person.”

Atukwatse says the imbalance between the evidence available to prosecutors and that available to defence lawyers can make allegations of mistreatment difficult to pursue.

“While the state can provide evidence of a post on social media, as lawyers, we cannot provide substantial evidence of how a client was abducted or tortured,” he says.

He also says that sometimes people are released, but the state leaves the charges hanging over them.

“Later on, the state loses interest, but there’s no formal withdrawal of charges, which means you may be out but not completely free.”

Army spokesperson Colonel Chris Magezi says allegations of unlawful conduct should be supported by evidence. He says the military operates within the law and works with police and intelligence agencies when necessary.

“We do everything in accordance with the law,” he says.

Magezi says suspects accused of violent crimes are brought before courts and that security agencies monitor social media. He rejects the suggestion that people are being disappeared unlawfully.

“The rest is political and not necessarily people being disappeared. If they disappear, they appear in court,” he says.

He also points to laws governing defamation.

“We have laws on defamation,” he says. “If you are going to say things about someone and you cannot substantiate it, you could be arrested.”

The ultimate fate of the online critics remains in the air: Opoloje was granted bail on October 14, but the criminal charge against her remains. Andrew was also released on bail, but he says the threats and intimidation still loom over him.

Emmanuel says he still does not even know where his son is being held. “I do not know where my son is,” he says.

articles.title: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results
articles.summary: Iran’s top negotiator says US voters sent a “NO TO WAR” message, as Trump’s Democratic opponents take Congress.
articles.body:
Democrats in the United States have scored a major victory in midterm elections, taking control of both chambers of Congress in a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

The results are being carefully watched outside the US, as foreign leaders consider how the new political reality in Washington could affect US foreign policy – from the conflict with Iran to the Russia-Ukraine war and trade relations.

Trump himself has acknowledged the US-Israel war on Iran likely impacted his party’s poor performance in the elections, saying voters were probably not ready “for the short-term consequence of the price of gasoline”.

Here are the latest reactions from world leaders, as the scale of the Democratic victory continues to emerge:

European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose said the US results left her “cautiously optimistic on Europe’s behalf”.

“Not because everything now ⁠⁠changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and ⁠⁠relations with the rest of the world,” said Schaldemose in a post on X.

“But the EU must continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That’s not up for debate,” she added.

Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also the chief negotiator in talks with the US, said voters had rejected conflict.

“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” wrote Ghalibaf in a post on X.

“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added.

Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile, said partisan shifts in Washington would not alter the US’s “hostility” towards Tehran.

“If there are still those who harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system could change through party or factional shifts, or who believe that making concessions to the US could persuade it to abandon its hostility towards the Iranian people, they are gravely mistaken,” said Khamenei in a statement shared by Iranian state media.

There was no immediate reaction from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a Trump ally whose coalition lost its own majority in Israel’s parliament in elections last week.

However, opposition figure Yair Golan, whose party is in a coalition seeking to replace Netanyahu , said the US vote reveals “just how toxic Netanyahu has become” among US Democrats and Republicans alike.

He warned that if Netanyahu and his far-right government remain in power, Israel would be on “a path toward international sanctions, global isolation, and a confrontation with the United States – our most important friend and ally.”

Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid, also part of the anti-Netanyahu coalition, said the US vote effectively ruled out “any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu”.

Health Minister James Frith stressed that the UK would maintain steady, strong ties with Washington despite an apparent “seismic shift in domestic politics for the Americans”.

“The change of emphasis of power in the States is frequent,” Frith told British media. “But the mainstay of the relationship with the UK Government, as its closest ally, is unwavering and unchanging.”

“So I don’t expect it to change the nature of the relationship at all; it remains very strong,” he added.

Finance Minister Roland Lescure said France would wait to see whether Trump, who remains in control of US foreign policy, adjusts his approach.

“Either he decides to rise above the fray – acknowledging that ‌‌changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly ‌‌affect people – and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement, or he does not,” Lescure told French TV. “Frankly, this is something we will need to keep an eye on in the ⁠⁠coming days.”

Left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the US Democrats’ landslide victory was emblematic of the “unravelling” of the global far right.

“It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will soon happen in Spain,” said Sanchez, whose own premiership is at stake in snap elections he called for November 29 .

Sanchez said US voters had rejected policies that “only ‌‌impoverish”, as well as hate, sexism, climate change denialism and “the privileges of the elites”.

Government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said US-Greek relations would not be affected by the election results.

“Greek-American relations will remain strong,” he told local media. “The United States is our strategic ally, and this will continue for major projects ⁠⁠and all major agreements. Nothing will be affected by this outcome. It is obvious that we respect every outcome. The conclusions are clear.”

Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov stressed the need to wait for the final results of US elections to come into focus, but noted that leaders in the US Democratic Party had a “sharply negative” approach to relations with Moscow.

Russia’s position on Ukraine and broader foreign policy “is not based on short-term considerations and, naturally, does not depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other countries,” Ryabkov was quoted by Russian state media as saying.

“We will continue our work in accordance with the directives of the President of the Russian Federation,” he added.

Kremlin spokesman ⁠Dmitry Peskov said Moscow hoped the US midterm results would not impact Trump’s “peacemaking efforts”.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing would continue its “constructive strategic relationship” with the US, stressing that US elections are a “domestic affair”.

“China is willing to work with the US to safeguard and implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, strengthen communication, properly manage differences and expand cooperation, build a constructive strategic relationship based on respect and equality,” Mao told reporters in Beijing.

Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said whatever the outcome of the US vote, “the Japan-US alliance the is the cornerstone of Japan’s foreign and security policy.”

“As the international situation becomes turbulent and increasingly uncertain, a strong Japan-US alliance is essential for maximising Japan’s national interests and for peace and stability in the international community,” Kihara said at a press briefing.

⁠President Cyril Ramaphosa, who has clashed with Trump over the US president’s promotion of debunked claims of a white genocide in South Africa, said the election marks “a new era in world relations”.

“We have seen that the ⁠⁠Democrats have taken ⁠⁠control of the Senate and of ⁠⁠the House, and ⁠⁠the ⁠⁠people of America have spoken,” Ramaphosa told ‌‌reporters.

articles.title: Children spending too long on maths app TT Rockstars, MP warns
articles.summary: The makers of the popular times table game say they are bringing in curfews and limits to screen time.
articles.body:
Concerns have been raised with the government about the amount of time primary school children are spending on a game designed to make learning times tables fun.

TT Rockstars, which allows children to compete with their classmates for virtual coins and rock-star themed characters and outfits, is widely used by schools for maths homework.

Labour MP Emily Darlington said the app and others like it could be harming children's development because it rewards them for "length of time rather than quality of time spent online".

Bruno Reddy, founder of the firm behind TT Rockstars, said he shared concerns about screen time and was working with schools to bring in curfews and time limits.

He said the company discourages long sessions, adding: "Every game in TTRS is deliberately short, and our characters remind children to take regular breaks.

"The rule of thumb we give schools is: three minutes, four or five times a week. In September, a typical child played on three days, for about six minutes each time."

He said that from 24 November "every school will have a curfew and a daily time limit switched on, and leaderboards switched off as default".

Darlington told BBC News that while education technology, or EdTech, can have a place in the classroom "when gamification is used, children spend hours online to 'earn' the latest outfit".

"Parents are concerned that this causes conflict on time spent on devices and the pressure to perform against classmates," she added, and this could deter them from taking part in real life, rather than screen-based, activities.

The Milton Keynes Central MP raised concerns about TT Rockstars on Tuesday at the Commons Science Committee, which is investigating the impact of screen time and digital devices on children's brain development.

The company behind TT Rockstars, Maths Circle, says that the app and a similar programme for addition and subtraction, Numbots, is used in 17,000 schools and over 100,000 households.

Reddy, a former maths teacher, said TT Rockstars had been designed to "boost learning in the classroom: recognising progress, celebrating achievement and making learning enjoyable".

He added: "We've deliberately steered away from features designed to keep children playing, such as streaks, random rewards, chat messages, loot boxes or notifications.

"There's no advertising and schools pay the same subscription however much their students play, so we have no commercial reason to want children on screen for longer."

The government is in the process of drawing up guidelines for schools and parents on the amount of time five to 16-year-olds should spend on screens.

At the committee, early years education minister Paul Waugh said: "Gamification isn't the way to learn.

"That's the propaganda they [EdTech companies] will give you but it is all about driving their screen time and their screen use. So it's profit driven."

He said there were "ways of making learning fun" that did not involve "competition with yourself or with someone else" and EdTech should be about supporting teachers and not replacing them.

It comes amid growing calls for the use of EdTech in the classroom to be limited.

Charlotte Ashton, co-founder of Generation Focus, which campaigns for smartphone-free schools, said: "Increasingly parents and teachers are saying no to Ed Tech because for the vast majority of digital 'learning tools' there's very little evidence they actually improve learning and growing evidence they can be harmful."

She added: "Not all tech is bad, but until we are confident that new digital tools improve children's learning without doing harm or imposing unintended consequences we are supporting schools to stick to proven teaching methods."

articles.title: Oxford cinema shortlisted as UK's best as it fights for future
articles.summary: The Ultimate Picture Palace in Oxford is nominated for the 2026 Cinema of the Year award.
articles.body:
One of the UK's oldest independent cinemas has been shortlisted for a prestigious award recognising the best in the country.

On Tuesday, the Ultimate Picture Palace (UPP) in Oxford was revealed as one of five nominees for the 2026 Cinema of the Year award at the British Independent Film Awards (BIFA).

More than 70 cinemas across the country entered the competition, with nearly 50,000 votes cast by cinemagoers.

The UPP was first founded in 1911 and is one of the UK's oldest purpose-built cinemas, but the nomination comes as it fights for its long-term future .

Those nominating the cinema for the award said it was a "beautiful, lovingly cared for" site that was "committed to the celebration of film in all its forms".

"The UPP is a gem that must continue to be protected and preserved for all to enjoy for many years to come," another added.

Since it was founded , the cinema has been screening a mix of independent, international and classic films in its single-screen auditorium.

It reopened in 1997 after a brief closure in 1994 and has operated as one of the UK's oldest purpose-built cinemas.

The cinema became community-owned in 2022 when 1,200 residents took a stake in it and raised £366,585.

Alastair Phillips, chair of the UPP, said the BIFA nomination "proves how important the Ultimate Picture Palace is, not just to our large and diverse Oxford audience but to the whole nation".

"We genuinely hope to secure the future of this very special cinema in the home which was built for it, for generations to come," he added.

Despite the award recognition, the cinema said it faced an "uncertain future" with its landlord, Oriel College, "currently unwilling to commit to its long-term future in the building".

Its current lease runs until 2037, which the UPP said was "too short" to secure funding for much-needed work to modernise the building.

More than 24,000 people have so far signed a petition calling for Oriel College to secure the future of the cinema.

Earlier this year, the University of Oxford college said it had "no plans to extend the lease at this early stage" in the tenancy, which began in 2022.

"We are very proud of our heritage cinema and are in dialogue with the new managers about how to ensure it remains open to the wider public," it added.

articles.title: Why are Europe’s governments struggling to respond to growing protests?
articles.summary: Protests intensify as governments prioritise security measures over addressing underlying social and economic concerns.
articles.body:
Protests across Europe show no sign of abating.

They subside on certain days, only to flare up a few days later. Largely led by young people, demonstrations have swept across at least eight European countries, driven by grievances ranging from school conditions and the cost of diesel to a deeper sense of insecurity about the future – and the feeling that opportunities are increasingly out of reach.

“They are plural and uncoordinated, with no single leader or programme,” said Alberto Alemanno, professor of European Union law and policy at HEC Paris Business School. “So it’s less a rejection of one policy and more a signal that people no longer trust the system to deliver. That’s why they are so critical.”

For governments, addressing discontent is proving difficult. Experts say there is no easy fix, and that many have so far struggled to offer answers beyond a show of force. The protests are likely to continue, they warn.

“Where there has been a reaction, the focus is on public order and security,” Alemanno said. “Part of the reason is that, like any popular protest, these movements include or attract small violent minorities . They dominate the headlines and risk undermining legitimate claims.”

Rallies continue because they are increasingly about more than individual grievances, said Donatella della Porta, a political science professor at the Scuola Normale Superiore in Florence. While governments have tried to address some of the protesters’ material demands, they have failed to grasp the broader political concerns driving the demonstrations.

“At this point, protests are no longer just about investing more in the school system. There are also fundamental issues, including military spending, governments’ alliance with [United States President Donald] Trump, the rising cost of gasoline and the war in Iran,” she said. “ The issue of Palestine is also very central to these protests.”

This week, protesters have continued to blockade several high schools and universities in France, where students have been pushing for better conditions, more teachers and the replacement of Parcoursup, an admission system that some say is discriminatory.

In Germany, metal and electrical workers have gone on strike while students have demonstrated over fears of the return of conscription. In Belgium, firefighters marched through Brussels, demanding more staff and better equipment. And on Friday in Italy, the USB union brought tens of thousands of people together, calling for a reduction in military spending.

France’s Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Monday that some measures to meet students’ demands have been adopted, including capping class sizes to 28 for the first year of high school, creating 10,000 places in higher technician programmes, and transforming Parcoursup.

Other measures require in-depth work between now and the end of December, he said on X. But the announcements have failed to quell the protests. On Tuesday, dozens of schools remained blockaded and several universities were disrupted, according to French media.

A nationwide strike over wages, the cost of living and public services is also expected on November 5.

In Spain, massive protests swept through the country for weeks over a housing crisis, triggered by the eviction and subsequent death of an 87-year-old pensioner from her lifelong home. On Tuesday, police dismantled a sprawling tent camp in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square.

Officials said the eviction took place overnight “without incident or episodes of violence”, reporting that 334 people were removed and two arrested.

In a post on Telegram, protest organisers lamented “a violent police operation” that they said left several people injured.

The government has approved new housing measures, including limits on rent increases and temporary protections against eviction for some vulnerable tenants.

But these promises have done little to dissuade protesters, who are planning a general strike over housing rights and the cost of living on November 11.

In Italy, after violence broke out during protests two weeks ago, the government of far-right leader Giorgia Meloni tightened security measures. “Violent participation” in a demonstration – by joining a group of five or more people and throwing stones, firecrackers or sticks – was made a criminal offence that could result in up to five years in prison and a fine of up to 20,000 euros ($22,500). Italy also made parents liable for damage caused by their children and adopted a policy of preventive detention of children.

The growing emphasis on public order has raised concerns among human rights organisations, which warn that European governments risk treating social discontent as a security threat rather than addressing the grievances behind it.

In a statement in October, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk raised serious concerns about the state responses to protests across Europe and the unnecessary and excessive use of force against protesters, including children.

Following the use of tear gas and stun grenades, among others, by French police against young protesters, Human Rights Watch said the government should “listen to the demands of young people on the streets”.

Della Porta said governments risk further alienating protesters by responding to demonstrations primarily through policing and repression.

“They can start by doing concrete things, such as recognising the right to protest and not sending police in a counterinsurgency-style approach to repress students,” she said.

Several European governments face significant fiscal constraints, while simultaneously increasing defence spending and investing in security. They now find themselves having to respond to demands for better public services, affordable housing and higher living standards while their budgets are increasingly stretched.

The fiscal constraints are particularly visible in some of Europe’s largest economies. Italy’s public debt is projected to reach 138.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026, limiting its room for additional spending. France faces an even more immediate budgetary squeeze, with its deficit forecast at 5.4 percent of GDP, well above the EU’s 3 percent limit. Spain, meanwhile, has struggled to secure parliamentary approval for a new budget, forcing the government to roll over its 2023 spending plans.

These pressures come as governments are trying to increase defence spending, while citizens are demanding more investment in housing, education and public services.

There is no easy option, Alemanno said, and “money is only part of the answer.”

“People will tolerate hard trade-offs if they are explained and if citizens have a say in them. Ignoring them is what fuels anger.”

articles.title: Celebrity hairstylist John Frieda dies at 75
articles.summary: John Frieda, the British celebrity hairstylist behind the Frizz Ease brand, has died, according to a statement posted to his Instagram on Tuesday.
articles.body: John Frieda, the British celebrity hairstylist behind the Frizz Ease brand, has died, according to a statement posted to his Instagram on Tuesday. He was 75. Frieda’s cause of death was not immediately clear. “It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our dear John passed away peacefully …. surrounded by his family,” the statement said. “John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry,” the statement continued. “He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better. His talent and passion touched so many, and his legacy will live on in every single one of us. We will continue to do him proud,” it added. Throughout his career, Frieda worked with some of the biggest celebrity names, including Princess Diana, pop superstar Madonna, former first lady Jackie Kennedy Onassis, The Beatles, actors Sarah Jessica Parker and Scarlett Johansson, among several others. Frieda was born in 1951 in London. At the time, his father owned a west London salon. Frieda told The Standard newspaper in 2012 that his dad had wanted him to become a doctor, but Frieda pursued a career in hair to get out of studying. He worked his way up through the London hairstyling scene, working alongside other big names in the business and styling models for Vogue fashion shoots. More than 30 years ago, he opened his first salon in London and went on to open branches in Los Angeles and New York City. In the 1990s, Frieda launched the Frizz Ease brand with a serum meant to tame frizzy hair. The brand has since grown in global popularity, with a whole line of products — sold in drug stores and salons across the world. Frieda married Scottish pop singer and actor Lulu in 1976. The couple had one son together and later divorced. He entered into a relationship with Avery Agnelli — the widow of Fiat heir Giovanni Agnelli — in the early 2000s, and the pair married in 2019. With Agnelli, Frieda shares two children and a stepdaughter. “Today we lost the best man to ever exist,” his stepdaughter, Asia Agnelli Lagrange, said in a brief tribute online. “I share this because I know he touched the lives of so many.”

articles.title: 'Dialled wrong number, season of dharna': CJI's quip at man seeking rotation of SC-ST reserved seats
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Wednesday quipped at a petitioner to organise public protests and demonstrations while rejecting his plea
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant on Wednesday quipped at a petitioner to organise public protests and demonstrations while rejecting his plea seeking mandatory rotation of seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in Parliament and state assemblies.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana upheld the Allahabad high court order validating Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, which provides for the identification of reserved constituencies in areas where the proportion of SC/ST residents is comparatively high.The Supreme Court, however, said the petitioner was free to approach public representatives and persuade them to adopt the principle of rotation."You are dialling the wrong number. This is a season of dharna, protest etc. You should also do the same," Bar and Bench quoted CJI Surya Kant as saying in a lighter vein."This is also a good ground for protest," he added.During the hearing, Justice Bagchi said that in a multiparty democracy, voters are expected to make electoral choices based on political ideologies rather than caste or religious considerations."In a political democracy, there are multiple political parties having different ideologies. The voters are expected to vote for the party, not for the religion. You may like or dislike a particular political ideology. Who is representing that ideology becomes irrelevant. You vote for that ideology. So that also defeats your argument," Justice Bagchi said.The bench also distinguished between the right to vote and any claimed right to contest an election from a particular constituency. It observed that candidates belonging to the general category remain eligible to contest from constituencies that are not reserved.The petitioner, Jagdish Singh, had challenged the continued reservation of his constituency for Scheduled Castes, claiming that it had remained reserved for nearly seven decades since its creation.He argued that the absence of a rotation mechanism violated Articles 14, 15 and 19 of the Constitution and restricted voters' electoral choices by limiting the candidates they could elect to members of the SC community.He further claimed that the existing arrangement benefited a handful of political families rather than advancing the interests of the wider community.Seeking a mechanism similar to the rotational reservation provided for panchayats and municipalities under Articles 243D and 243T of the Constitution, the petitioner urged the bench to direct periodic rotation of SC/ST-reserved constituencies.Justice Bagchi, however, disagreed with the argument that candidates from the majority community would anyway get elected in constituencies with a high SC population, making reservation unnecessary."That proceeds on the idea that a majority community will vote on community or caste lines. They may not vote on community and caste lines. The High Court cannot judicially pronounce on a democratic choice. That is for the voters to decide," Justice Bagchi said.The bench clarified that it could not rewrite the Constitution or the statute by introducing a rotation requirement that finds no mention in Articles 330 and 332 or the Delimitation Act.The Allahabad high court had held that Articles 330 and 332 merely prescribe the number of reserved seats in proportion to the population and leave the methodology for identifying reserved constituencies to Parliament under Article 327.It had found Section 9(1)(c) neither ultra vires nor violative of fundamental rights, ruling that courts cannot issue a mandamus directing the legislature to introduce a rotation provision.While acknowledging that rotation could better advance social and political justice by allowing SC/ST candidates to contest even from constituencies with smaller reserved-category populations, the high court had emphasised that the policy decision rests exclusively with Parliament.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
