articles.body: The US midterm elections have changed the political balance in Washington, with Democrats winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in a setback for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. For Indian-Americans, the outcome raises questions about whether the change in congressional power will translate into any meaningful shift in policies affecting their lives.The result comes amid growing concerns within the community over immigration restrictions, employment opportunities and questions of identity and belonging. These concerns have become particularly significant for Indian professionals, who form a substantial part of the US technology workforce, but extend beyond skilled migration to the wider treatment of immigrants.The shift is notable because Indian-Americans had shown greater openness to Republicans in the 2024 presidential election. Trump's second term, however, has brought a series of policy changes and political developments that have tested that support.Democrats win Congress: What changes for Trump's agenda?Democratic victories have given the party control of both chambers of Congress for the first time during Trump's second term. The new Congress will have greater powers to investigate the administration, summon officials for hearings, scrutinise immigration enforcement and challenge budgetary decisions.For Indian-Americans concerned about immigration restrictions, this creates a political counterweight to the administration. Democratic lawmakers can question the implementation of measures affecting skilled foreign workers, including H-1B sponsorship and visa scrutiny.However, Trump retains the power to veto any bill passed by Congress, and Democrats would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override his veto.The immediate significance, therefore, is greater scrutiny and a more difficult legislative environment for Trump, rather than an automatic rollback of his immigration agenda.Are Indian-Americans moving away from Trump? What the data showsThe October 2026 Carnegie Endowment for International Peace survey offers an indication of how these concerns are reflected in voting preferences. Conducted in partnership with YouGov between October 7 and 27 among 1,000 Indian-American adults, it found that 62% of Indian-American citizens intended to vote for Democratic congressional candidates, compared with 19% for Republicans. Another 12% were undecided. The voting analysis was based on 861 US citizens.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The survey also points to a distinction between party identity and voting preference. Forty-six per cent of respondents identified as Democrats, 19% as Republicans and 26% as independents. These figures were virtually unchanged from January 2026, even as voting intentions shifted towards Democratic candidates.Another finding is particularly relevant to the idea of a vote against Trump. Among respondents who intended to support a Democratic congressional candidate, 35% said their primary motivation was opposition to the Republican candidate or party, rather than support for the Democratic side. The remaining 65% cited support for the Democratic candidate or party as their main motivation.Here are some factors that directly affected Indians:H-1B restrictions: A direct hit on Indian professionalsThe H-1B programme is one of the most consequential areas for Indian-Americans because of the community's strong presence in the US technology and professional workforce. People born in India accounted for 69.9% of all approved H-1B petitions in fiscal year 2025, or 283,772 of 406,348 approvals, according to US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) data.The Trump administration has sought to make the programme more expensive and selective. It introduced a $100,000 payment requirement for certain new H-1B petitions involving workers outside the US, with specified exceptions. In September 2026, Trump extended the restriction for another 12 months, until September 21, 2027. However, federal courts have blocked its implementation, and the fee is not currently being collected.The administration has argued that the programme has been exploited by employers to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign labour. In the September 2026 proclamation, Trump said it had been used to “replace, not supplement” American workers. The measure has, however, raised concerns among Indian professionals and employers over the cost and uncertainty of hiring foreign workers.Deportations: Crackdown beyond skilled migrationThe administration's immigration enforcement has also affected Indians outside the skilled-worker visa system. The first US deportation flight carrying 104 Indian nationals under Trump's second administration arrived in Amritsar in February 2025. Images of deportees in handcuffs and leg restraints triggered criticism in India, with the government raising concerns with Washington over the use of restraints, particularly on women.The ministry of external affairs said 3,567 Indian nationals were deported from the US in 2025 and another 1,273 between January 1 and July 22, 2026.These figures concern deportations and should not be conflated with legal migrants or H-1B workers. But the operations have brought the wider immigration crackdown into focus for Indian families and communities, including those with relatives living in the US.Jobs, layoffs and scrutiny of Indian IT companiesEmployment concerns have added another dimension. Layoffs in the US technology sector can leave H-1B workers with limited time to find another qualifying employer or change their immigration status. This makes job security particularly important for foreign professionals whose ability to remain in the country is tied to their employment.The administration's scrutiny has also extended to employers. In October 2026, the US Labour Department suspended eight technology companies, including Indian IT firms Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech, from the Permanent Labour Certification programme, or PERM. The action prevents the companies from filing new or processing pending applications under the employment-based green-card process.The move does not mean these companies have been removed from the H-1B programme, nor does it automatically cancel the visas of their existing employees. But it can affect foreign workers seeking permanent residency through employer sponsorship.The administration has defended its actions by alleging that some employers have used the system at the expense of American workers. On October 8, Vice-President JD Vance described foreign workers brought in through the process as “foreign indentured servants” while announcing the action against Microsoft and other companies. Microsoft disputed the administration's characterisation of its H-1B filings, saying most were for extensions or changes in status of existing employees.US-India ties: Another source of dissatisfactionUS-India relations have also become a point of concern among Indian-Americans. A Carnegie survey conducted between November 2025 and January 2026 found that 55% of respondents disapproved of Trump's handling of bilateral ties, compared with 20% who approved. A quarter expressed no opinion.Concerns over trade, tariffs and the future of strategic cooperation have added to the unease, particularly among those with business, family or professional links to both countries. The administration's approach to India has therefore become another factor shaping perceptions of Trump's presidency.Racism and MAGA rhetoricBeyond immigration rules and employment, the political climate has raised concerns about identity and belonging among Indian-Americans. Trump has repeatedly portrayed immigration as a threat, often without distinguishing between undocumented migrants and those legally living in the US.In his final television speech before the midterms on November 3, election day, Trump defended his immigration crackdown, claiming that millions had entered the US under the previous administration, “many criminals and murderers”. He also alleged that migrants had been released from prisons in countries across Africa, Asia and South America.When I took over, the border was open. We were having millions and millions of people pour in, many criminals and murderers.A controversy involving Bo French, the Republican nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, brought these tensions into focus. French posted a photograph of University of Texas students of South Asian origin celebrating a football victory, claiming it showed how many Americans had been “displaced by foreigners”. In another post, he wrote: “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”Also read: Texas railroad commission - Bo French, Republican who sparked anti-India row, defeated by Democrat Jon RosenthalThe posts drew criticism from students and several Texas Republicans. The students' citizenship status was not established, but the incident highlighted how people can be perceived as outsiders based on their appearance.A Carnegie Endowment for International Peace survey conducted between November 25, 2025, and January 6, 2026, found that half of Indian-American respondents had experienced discrimination since the start of 2025. Forty-eight per cent said they encountered racist social media posts targeting Indians or Indian-Americans somewhat or very often, while one in four said they had been called a slur.The impact has been visible even among Indian-Americans who are US citizens. In Frisco, Texas, Burt Thakur, a US citizen, Navy veteran and Trump supporter serving on the city council, told The Texas Tribune that he had faced racist remarks directed at him and the wider Indian community.In April 2026, Trump himself shared a podcast transcript describing India and China as “hellhole” countries and questioning the loyalty and integration of immigrants from those countries.Indian-origin candidates: Wins and losses in US midtermsThe election also saw several Indian-origin Democratic candidates secure victories, while Republican Vivek Ramaswamy lost the Ohio governor's race despite Trump's backing. The results add to the picture of Indian-Americans making their presence felt in US politics, but with contrasting fortunes across party lines.Democrat Pia Dandiya won Florida's 22nd Congressional District, while Suhas Subramanyam secured re-election from Virginia's 10th Congressional District. Maryland Lieutenant Governor Aruna Miller also won another term alongside Democratic Governor Wes Moore.Other prominent Indian-American Democratic lawmakers, including Ro Khanna, Ami Bera and Pramila Jayapal, also secured victories.Ramaswamy's defeat, alongside the wins by Indian-origin Democrats, is also significant in this regard, even if indirectly.Also read: Indian-American candidates shine in US midterms 2026: Who won from where? Full listH-1B workers: Will Democrats be able to offer relief?The H-1B programme has an annual statutory cap of 65,000 visas, with another 20,000 places for applicants holding advanced degrees from US institutions. It allows American employers to recruit foreign professionals for speciality occupations generally requiring at least a bachelor's degree or equivalent.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();India has a significant presence in the programme. In FY2025, Indian-born beneficiaries accounted for 77.6% of approved petitions for continuing employment, compared with 50.3% of approvals for initial employment. Computer-related occupations accounted for 62% of all approved petitions, underlining the programme's importance to the technology workforce.Another major change is the wage-weighted selection system, effective February 27, 2026. It gives applicants in higher-paid positions a greater chance of selection in the cap-subject process, replacing the traditional random selection system. This could affect entry-level applicants and employers relying on lower-wage positions.The long green-card wait is another challenge. USCIS data as of June 2026 showed 356,360 approved Indian EB-2 petitions and 106,214 EB-3 petitions awaiting visa availability. These are approved employment-based petitions awaiting a visa number, not simply pending applications. The backlog can leave Indian professionals dependent on temporary work status for years.With control of Congress, Democrats can use hearings and oversight to examine the impact of these changes and push for legislative alternatives. However, reversing administrative rules such as the wage-weighted selection system would require action beyond a change in congressional leadership, as immigration agencies remain under the executive branch.The midterm results do not establish a permanent shift in Indian-American political loyalties. But concerns over immigration, jobs, discrimination and US-India ties have made the community's support less predictable. Whether Democrats can turn this into lasting support will depend on how effectively they address these concerns, while Republicans will have to reckon with changing voter preferences.You use AI every day. articles.title: Spokane real estate magnate Harlan Douglass left an estate of about $600 million; on October 26 a judge ruled two of his three children financially exploited him as he lived with dementia, barring them from inheriting
articles.summary: The fortune, accumulated in property over decades, is now at the centre of an extraordinary family inheritance battle over manipulation, disputed
articles.body: The fortune, accumulated in property over decades, is now at the centre of an extraordinary family inheritance battle over manipulation, disputed documents, and a father whose failing memory made him increasingly dependent on others. The November 2023 death of Spokane property magnate Harlan Douglass left an estimated $600 million. A bitter legal battle ensued between his three children over his fortune. In a major ruling on Oct. 26, 2026, a Washington judge finds that two of his children financially exploited their father while he was vulnerable with dementia and Alzheimer's. The decision effectively disqualifies them from receiving an inheritance, potentially leaving their older brother in control of a fortune that could exceed $1 billion when disputed assets are included.A family fortune divided by a disputed willAccording to The Spokesman-Review, Harlan's estate included a substantial real estate portfolio valued at approximately $350 million, alongside promissory notes worth another $155 million. His three children, Harley Douglass, Lanzce Douglass and Stacey Douglass Boies, had been at the centre of a prolonged dispute over how these assets should be distributed.The disagreement intensified after Harlan's will was changed in 2019. An earlier version, signed in 2018, divided his estate equally among his three children. The revised document, however, allocated 65% to Lanzce, 35% to Stacey and just $1,000 to Harley.Harley claimed his younger siblings used their father's mental decline to influence his decisions and take more of the family's wealth.How dementia affected the caseHarlan seemed to have had mental issues for years before signing the dispute papers. According to The Spokesman-Review, he experienced increasing memory problems from 2016 onwards, followed by confusion with numbers, difficulty understanding documents and trouble managing everyday responsibilities.By 2019, he increasingly depended on others to read paperwork, organise his medication, arrange appointments and handle financial matters.In her 58-page ruling, Spokane Superior Court Judge Jacquelyn High-Edward found that these circumstances made Harlan particularly vulnerable to outside influence. She concluded that Lanzce and Stacey had used this vulnerability to get him to sign documents that they had prepared, without ensuring he understood their contents, explains Yahoo News,The judge also invalidated promissory notes worth approximately $155 million that would have benefited the younger siblings and their children. Property assignments involving four real estate holdings were also voided, restoring the assets to Harley.An earlier inheritance dispute raised similar questionsThe latest ruling was not the family's first courtroom battle over an inheritance. Yahoo News reports that a similar dispute followed the death of Harlan's wife, Maxine Douglass, in 2016.Her 2008 will had allocated 50% of her estate to Harley, 40% to Stacey and 10% to Lanzce. However, a document prepared in 2019, known as the Hamilton Deed, subsequently transferred much of her estate towards the younger siblings and removed Harley as a beneficiary.A court later found that Lanzce had orchestrated the preparation of the document, which was signed by Harlan when witnesses observed him struggling to stay awake and follow what was happening. In 2023, a judge ruled in Harley's favour, invalidating the deed.The two inheritance battles have therefore involved overlapping allegations about the influence exerted on Harlan as his health declined.What happens to the billion-dollar legacy?The October ruling represents a significant victory for Harley, but the final distribution of the family fortune is not entirely settled.As reported by The Spokesman-Review, the 2018 will provides for an equal division among the three children. However, with Lanzce and Stacey now barred from inheriting because of the financial exploitation finding, the court may still need to determine whether their respective shares should pass to their own children or be absorbed by Harley's inheritance.Yahoo News reports that the disputed estate, property holdings and promissory notes could take the total value involved beyond $1 billion.The ruling also marks another painful chapter for a family whose relationships have deteriorated over years of legal proceedings. Harlan, who built one of Spokane's most significant real estate fortunes, died at 86. His legacy is now being shaped as much by the courtrooms as by the properties and business interests he left behind.Images Courtesy: istock and The Spokesman-ReviewYou use AI every day. articles.title: Ed Sheeran received approval in October 2026 to restore six deteriorating barns on a historic Suffolk farm for his private music archive, alongside previously approved plans to turn an old piggery into studios
articles.summary: Ed Sheeran has received planning approval to restore six deteriorating barns on his historic Suffolk farm, creating private storage and archive space for
articles.body: Ed Sheeran has received planning approval to restore six deteriorating barns on his historic Suffolk farm, creating private storage and archive space for his music collection. The decision, reported by the East Anglian Daily Times and Future Positive, adds another chapter to the singer’s carefully expanding countryside project, which also includes previously approved plans to convert an old piggery into recording studios.The barns form part of Sheeran’s Grade II-listed farm in Suffolk, where planning permission was granted by Mid Suffolk District Council in October 2026. Rather than introducing a new standalone development, the scheme is designed to bring neglected 19th-century outbuildings back into use while retaining their historic character. Read more about it here, as per the reports:A private archive in SuffolkThe approved plans will see the six barns used solely as storage and archive space for Sheeran and his family. According to the application, there will be no additional vehicles, lighting or equipment installed, reinforcing the private and low-impact nature of the project.For an artist whose career has produced years of recordings, demos, artwork, instruments and memorabilia, the archive represents more than a practical storage solution. It offers a secure home for the material history of Sheeran’s work, kept close to the Suffolk landscape that has long influenced his life and music. The restoration will focus on returning the buildings to something close to their original form. Planning documents state that partially deteriorated or collapsed sections will be repaired in line with the original scale, design and appearance of the historic structures.Restoring rather than replacingThe barns are part of an established group of buildings within the farm’s existing residential setting. The planning officer’s report described the proposal as a sensitive restoration and continued ancillary use of those buildings, rather than unrelated new development in the countryside. Sheeran has committed to repairing and restoring the structures, adding windows, doors and staircases where necessary while preserving their original character. The approach suggests a deliberate effort to avoid turning the site into a glossy modern complex at the expense of its agricultural heritage.Earlier plans to connect the barns directly to the main farmhouse were dropped after pre-planning advice. That change appears to have helped the proposal align more closely with conservation expectations and the existing layout of the historic farm.Part of a wider music complexThe barn restoration sits alongside Sheeran’s previously approved plans to transform an old piggery on the estate into recording studios. Together, the projects point towards a private creative compound where the singer can store, revisit and potentially work on material in a setting far removed from a conventional city studio, the reports suggest.The wider development has drawn comparisons with EMI’s famous Abbey Road Studios in north London, where The Beatles recorded much of their most celebrated work. The comparison is understandable, although Sheeran’s Suffolk project appears intended primarily for personal use rather than as a commercial studio open to other artists.The singer already owns a 16-acre estate nearby, and the barns form part of what has become known locally as his expanding “Sheeranville” property. The new approval extends that vision while placing conservation and restoration at the centre of the plans.A careful balance with natureThe application was supported by ecologists, who noted a low flood risk and a positive impact on the historic farm. Their backing suggests that the project was assessed not only for its architectural impact but also for its effect on the surrounding environment.Work on other parts of the site has moved slowly because hand tools are being used and protected great crested newts are present. Their presence requires a special licence, reflecting the need to protect local wildlife during construction and restoration work.Sheeran has also pledged to create a species-rich flowering lawn featuring 19 types of flowers and to plant 12 fruit trees. These commitments add a ecological dimension to the project, framing it as an attempt to improve the site’s biodiversity as well as preserve its built heritage.What the approval meansThe decision gives Sheeran the green light to save buildings that might otherwise continue to deteriorate. By restoring the barns for archive use, the project gives them a clear future purpose while avoiding the sort of large-scale alteration that can erode the identity of a historic farm.It also reflects a wider trend among high-profile musicians who choose to build private creative spaces away from major cities. For Sheeran, whose connection to Suffolk is well known, the farm offers both privacy and a meaningful sense of place.The approval does not mean the work will happen overnight. Restoration of historic buildings is often slow, particularly when protected species, traditional materials and conservation requirements are involved. Still, the permission marks an important step towards turning a group of fading agricultural buildings into a lasting home for Sheeran’s musical legacy.A legacy rooted in SuffolkFor fans, the most intriguing aspect of the project is what it may eventually contain. While the archive will remain private, it could preserve the raw material behind one of Britain’s most successful contemporary songwriters, from early recordings to the documents and objects that trace the evolution of his career.For Suffolk, the scheme represents an investment in the careful repair of historic rural buildings. If completed as planned, the barns will remain recognisably part of their original farm setting, even as they take on a new role in the private world of one of the county’s most famous residents.The project is therefore less about creating a lavish celebrity retreat and more about giving old buildings a considered second life. In combining restoration, wildlife measures and a personal music archive, Ed Sheeran’s Suffolk plans offer a notably restrained vision of how heritage and creativity can coexist.You use AI every day. articles.title: Woolpots solar farm plan to be reconsidered after legal challenge
articles.summary: The Planning Inspectorate is set to examine the proposal on 25 November.
articles.body:
Plans to build a 126-acre (50 hectare) solar farm in North Yorkshire are to be reconsidered after a High Court judge quashed a previous decision to grant permission.

The Woolpots scheme, near the village of Husthwaite, was approved on appeal in October 2025, after being refused by North Yorkshire Council.

This was then overturned in August following a legal challenge from resident Philip Hewitson, who argued that the plan did not properly consider the impact on the landscape.

The Planning Inspectorate has now said the appeal will be reconsidered, with a hearing set for 25 November.

The scheme, proposed by Woolpots Solar Farm Ltd, includes solar panels capable of exporting around 32MW of electricity.

It would also incorporate a battery energy storage facility (BESS) with a capacity of 37MWh, comprising up to 32 battery containers and associated infrastructure, according to the Local Democracy Reporting Service .

The council initially refused permission over concerns about the impact on the surrounding landscape, views from the Howardian Hills and the loss of high-quality agricultural land.

The High Court decision does not mean the solar farm must be refused permission, but requires the appeal to be determined again.

Opponents say around 70% of the proposed development site comprises the best and most versatile agricultural land.

Husthwaite parish councillor Sarah Aspinall said there was growing concern about the concentration of solar developments across the wider Hambleton area.

She said: "There has also been a steady increase in the number of pending and approved solar and battery storage applications in the wider Hambleton area, with many concerned – both within and outside our parish – about cumulative impact and industrialisation of the countryside."

The applicant has not responded to requests from the Local Democracy Reporting Service to comment on the scheme.

articles.title: Mother and daughter die in suspected bear attack on Canada trail
articles.summary: A mother and daughter were found dead following a suspected grizzly bear attack on a trail in Canada.
articles.body: A mother and daughter were found dead following a suspected grizzly bear attack on a trail in Canada. The discovery was made near Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola after the family reported two people missing on Monday, the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said. One person was found dead Monday afternoon by search and rescue teams, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said. The second person’s remains were found Tuesday afternoon. Evidence suggests that a grizzly bear attack may have been involved in the deaths, Tyre said in a video statement on Facebook. No bears have been captured, and the public was asked to avoid the trail area. The Conservation Officer Service said it’s not clear how many bears may have been involved in the attack. Any bear that is determined to have been involved “will be dispatched in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines to protect public safety,” the agency said in a Facebook post. “Our thoughts are with the family of the victims during this tragic time. We are in contact with the family to offer any support we can as we continue to investigate this incident,” Tyre said. The Vancouver Sun identified the mother and her daughter as Jenny Balcarras, 48, and Selah Reed. The coroner’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. “Jenny was a wonderful artist,” her brother, Matt Balcarras, told the newspaper. He said she was in Bella Coola to work as an art therapist at a school. The trail the mother and daughter were on was very close to their home, Matt Balcarras said. The Central Coast Teachers Association said it was deeply saddened by the deaths. “Jenny devoted countless hours to connecting with the students she served and worked closely with teachers and other staff supporting their well-being,” the association said in a statement. “At the heart of her work was a commitment to building relationships and helping students feel known, heard, and supported.”

articles.title: A Houston couple lost their home in a 2001 foreclosure, yet signed a reverse mortgage in 2011; after an HOA foreclosure and a new buyer, a Texas appeals court reopened the fight over who had a valid claim
articles.summary: A long-running dispute over the ownership of a home in Houston has returned to court after a Texas appeals court reopened the case.
articles.body: A long-running dispute over the ownership of a home in Houston has returned to court after a Texas appeals court reopened the case. The ruling brings years of ownership claims, earlier foreclosures, and reverse mortgage agreements back into the legal process. The Fourteenth Court of Appeals of Texas reviewed the case under docket number 14-25-00470-CV. The court found that the competing claims over the property could not be settled through a summary judgment because important facts remained unclear. It overturned the lower court's decision that had ended the dispute and sent the case back for further legal proceedings. At the center of the case is a disagreement over who legally owns the home. A couple lost the property through foreclosure in 2001 but later took out a reverse mortgage against the same home in 2011. The property then faced another foreclosure started by a local homeowners association before a new buyer entered the picture.Decades of shifting titles and mortgagesThe property's ownership history includes a complicated series of deals and legal actions spanning twenty-five years. Court records show that the original homeowners lost their legal title to the home in a foreclosure sale in 2001. However, even after losing ownership on paper, the former owners continued to live in or maintain control of the property. Ten years later, in 2011, a financial institution arranged a reverse mortgage with the couple using the home as security. This created a major financial claim against the property. The agreement raised further legal questions because a mortgage is generally valid only if the person taking it out has the legal right to use the property as security. The dispute grew more complicated when the property became involved in a disagreement over unpaid fees owed to the local homeowners association. The association began its own foreclosure process to collect the unpaid charges. This led to a public auction, where a new buyer purchased the property's title. After the sale, the new owner faced competing legal claims from the mortgage company, which argued that it still had rights under the 2011 reverse mortgage agreement. These conflicting claims led to a lawsuit in a Harris County trial court. The judges initially granted summary judgment in favor of one of the parties claiming rights to the property.Appeals panel identifies unresolved questions of factThe Fourteenth Court of Appeals found that the trial court had made its decision too early. It ruled that the dispute could not be settled without first answering several important questions about the property's ownership history. In its opinion, the appeals court reviewed the validity and legal priority of the different property deeds, foreclosure sales, and recorded financial claims. Under Texas property law, a person generally cannot give a lender a valid legal claim against real estate unless that person has proper legal ownership or a recognized equitable interest in the property when the mortgage is signed. The judges pointed out that the ten-year gap between the 2001 foreclosure and the 2011 reverse mortgage raised serious questions about the property's ownership history. The court also noted that the later homeowners association foreclosure and the mortgage company's claims needed a full trial. These issues could not be properly settled through a shortened court process. In its decision, the court explained that important facts were still unclear. These included whether the 2011 mortgage lien could legally be enforced and whether the new buyer had valid legal rights after purchasing the property through the homeowners association's foreclosure sale.Broader legal implications for title safetyProperty law experts and real estate analysts say the case highlights major risks in property title searches and systems used to record financial claims against homes. When property records contain missing information or unconfirmed legal claims, both new buyers and financial institutions can face greater legal risks. In Texas, homeowners associations can use non-judicial foreclosure procedures to collect unpaid fees. However, these sales can create uncertainty over property ownership when earlier mortgages, existing financial claims, or problems with the title have not been properly reviewed. The Fourteenth Court of Appeals' decision makes clear that lower courts must carefully examine competing ownership claims before ruling that someone's property rights have ended. This is especially important when a property's history includes several foreclosures, mortgages, and changes in ownership. The lawsuit will now return to the Harris County district court for further evidence gathering and court hearings. The next stage will focus on establishing the property's exact ownership history after the 2001 foreclosure. The court will also need to decide whether the 2011 reverse mortgage created a legally enforceable claim against the home.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 18-year-old Aubrie Sink turned homemade jam sales at farmers’ markets into a freeze-dried candy business after investing her savings in a freeze dryer; her products are now sold at Disney World, Six Flags parks, and the Cincinnati Zoo
articles.summary: Aubrie Sink turned her childhood interest in making jam into a freeze-dried candy business, and now sells its products at Disney World.
articles.body: Aubrie Sink turned her childhood interest in making jam into a freeze-dried candy business, and now sells its products at Disney World. At 12, the Northern Kentucky teenager started making homemade jams, and by 2021 she was selling them at farmers’ markets and craft shows. She used the money from those sales to buy a freeze dryer after discovering the equipment on TikTok.Her freeze-dried sweets soon became more popular than her jams, prompting her to shift her focus to candy. According to the WPBF, Sink later expanded the business into a commercial kitchen and opened a storefront in Florence, Kentucky. Her products have since reached several attractions and retailers, while she continues to study full-time at the University of Kentucky.How Aubrie Sink’s early business ventures led her to freeze-dried candySink’s interest in business began before she started selling food. She said, "I've had a business since I was so young. I mean, even when I was 8 years old, I had a paper route, and I would go door to door.”By 2021, she was selling homemade jams under the name “Jammin’ with Aubrie” at farmers markets and craft shows. She did this at weekends while also taking part in competitive cheerleading. She used the money from the sales to invest in another idea.Sink said, "I saved up my money from doing that to buy a freeze dryer because I had been seeing it on TikTok, and so I was like, Mom, like, please let me do it. It took six months for her to let me buy a freeze dryer."A home-based venture grows into a commercial businessThe freeze dryer marked a change in the direction of Sink’s business. Her freeze-dried candy became more popular than the jams, leading her to move away from the “Jammin’” name and focus on “Freezin’”. The business grew beyond the scale of a home project. Sink moved into a commercial kitchen and opened a storefront in Florence, Kentucky.She said, "I had no idea it was going to take me. Like, I was just kind of doing it for fun.”"And I mean, I didn't expect it to grow this much, but I'm really happy I did."As of July 2026, the company employed 14 people, according to WPBF.Aubrie Sink takes her candy business from local markets to DisneyFreezin’ with Aubrie products are sold at Sink’s Florence storefront and several other destinations. These include the Cincinnati Zoo, Jungle Jim’s and Six Flags parks across the country.Sink said, "So now it's in Mission: Space, in Space Mountain and Magic Kingdom and Epcot. So yeah, it's so exciting.”"It's really shown me like, okay, well, maybe nothing is impossible."The Disney sales mark a major expansion for the business, which began with homemade jams sold at local markets and craft shows.What are Aubrie Sink’s plans for expanding her businessSink hopes to take the business into more Disney parks and expand its reach to the Disney Cruise Line. She also wants to grow a product line: “dirty soda” kits. The kits are already available at Jungle Jim’s, and Sink is considering further ways to develop the idea. articles.title: Former ‘Diddy’ prosecutor to lead Cornell sexual assault investigation
articles.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James announced Wednesday that a former federal prosecutor who oversaw the criminal case against Sean “Diddy” Combs will lead the investigation into an alleged 2024 sexual assault at a Cornell University fraternity house.
articles.body: New York Attorney General Letitia James announced Wednesday that a former federal prosecutor who oversaw the criminal case against Sean “Diddy” Combs will lead the investigation into an alleged 2024 sexual assault at a Cornell University fraternity house. Former federal prosecutor Jacqueline Kelly, a Cornell graduate, was also the first chief of the civil rights unit in the criminal division of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York. Kelly is now a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner, a firm that represented women who accused Jeffrey Epstein of sexual abuse. James, who was re-elected as the state’s top law enforcement official Tuesday, said in a statement that Kelly “is a seasoned prosecutor who has overseen numerous cases from investigation through trial.” “With her criminal legal expertise, commitment to public service, and judicial experience, I am confident that she will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation,” James added. In a statement, Kelly thanked James for the opportunity to lead the review that was ordered Oct. 1 by Gov. Kathy Hochul after the governor raised concerns that the local district attorney who originally considered charges did not do a proper assessment. “All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case,” Kelly said in a statement. “I look forward to lending my years of experience as a federal prosecutor to the Office of the Attorney General as we examine all available evidence.” A former Cornell student filed a lawsuit under the pseudonym Jane Doe in September, accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of plying her with drugs and sexually assaulting her after what was initially a consensual threesome at the chapter’s house on Oct. 19 and 20, 2024. The woman, who later dropped out of school, reported the incident to the university and to campus police in November 2024. Records reviewed by NBC News show that the Cornell University Police Department interviewed several witnesses and obtained other evidence. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten declined to bring charges after his office reviewed a six-page statement provided by Jane Doe, which the prosecutor said did not describe a potential crime. Records show that Van Houten’s team did not review additional statements from Jane Doe and others who were interviewed. Lawyers for two of the accused fraternity members have asked different state judges to disqualify James from leading the case on the basis that past comments she made on social media in support of Jane Doe exhibit a prejudgment and bias. Those requests are pending. James has said that her investigation will be fair and fact-based and that her social media remarks, which were made before she was appointed to handle the case, were based on empathy for the accuser. The office “is committed to a thorough investigation guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law,” James said in her statement announcing Kelly’s appointment. On the day James was appointed, her office said she was expected to recruit an outside attorney to assist in-house lawyers with the probe. Kelly is now set to bring a team from her law firm, which she joined as a partner last year. Her bio says she specializes in “high-profile regulatory or criminal investigations, as well as victims of sexual assault and other crimes.” Kelly also worked on a New York indictment against octogenarian fashion CEO Peter Nygard, who in 2024 was sentenced in Canada to 11 years in prison for sexual assaults. The ex-prosecutor also handled a case against Ricardo Cruciani, a pain management doctor accused of sexually abusing a number of patients in several states. In 2025, Kelly oversaw the prosecution that led to Combs’ conviction for transportation to engage in prostitution but ended in his acquittal of more serious sex trafficking and racketeering conspiracy counts. The disgraced entertainment executive is serving a 50-month federal prison sentence. One of the men accused in Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Winston Lee, is represented by Teny Geragos, who defended Combs at his federal trial. Geragos declined to comment on Kelly’s appointment.

articles.title: No regrets: Trump says Iran war justified despite polls drubbing
articles.summary: Trump acknowledges Iran war played role in defeats but says he would launch it again.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has acknowledged the impact of the United States’ attack on Iran and a sharp rise in prices on stunning Republican losses in midterm elections on Tuesday, but said the move was justified and denied responsibility for the rout.

“We actually have the greatest economy, but because of the gasoline price, people don’t see it as much as they would have without it. And the gasoline was caused by Iran,” he told Fox News in a televised phone interview late on Tuesday.

“People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline. I understand that. I don’t agree with it.”

Speaking to The Wall Street Journal about the Republican defeats , Trump said about the Iran war: “I did the right thing. I would have done it again.”

Republican strategist James Davis said the war contributed to the setbacks for the party but also to a lack of clear messaging.

“The war was definitely part of it and has helped shift the electorate toward Democrats. But the biggest issue was not the war itself, but the clear articulation of a strategy that gives people confidence in that strategy,” Davis told Al Jazeera.

The economic fallout from the conflict, including higher energy and especially diesel costs, had affected all sectors of the economy and intensified Americans’ concerns about affordability, he added.

Trump did not acknowledge any failings in his strategy, citing his absence from the ballot as the reason Republicans struggled to mobilise voters and blaming the defeated candidates themselves.

“I wasn’t on the ticket,” Trump said in an interview with The New York Times. “And because I wasn’t on the ticket, we couldn’t get enough people out to vote.”

Trump faulted the losing Republicans, many of whom he had handpicked and held multiple rallies for.

“Some of the candidates that I endorsed fought me,” he said, adding that “some of them had a lot of flaws, and obviously they were not acceptable to the voters”.

Commenting on the shock defeat of Texas Governor Greg Abbott, Trump lamented that his longtime ally had become a “Republican in name only,” without elaborating.

“If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost,” he said in a post to his social media platform Truth Social.

In a preview of his likely governing style over the next two years, the president also posted a picture of his trademark red cap emblazoned with the word “veto” to convey his determination to block legislation carried by the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress.

In the run-up to the losses, Trump repeatedly said presidents tend to lose midterm elections and had brushed off the suggestion that his policies had turned off voters.

Speaking to Fox News, Trump said he did not plan to make any changes to his cabinet after the rebuke from voters.

“It had nothing to do with my cabinet. It’s just a point in time. There was a mood in the air, I guess.”

In a conciliatory note, Trump said he wanted to work with Democrats but warned he would stand his ground as well.

“I think we’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll get along very well with them. If we don’t, we’ll be very tough on them; they’ll be very tough on us,” he said.

“Could I work with them on transgender mutilization of children?” he added. “No, I don’t think so. But I could work with them on many things.”

articles.title: Hungary opens secret police files, 47 years after fall of communism
articles.summary: Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish.
articles.body:
Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule.

Critics say it has come too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members.

The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution.

"I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity," Prime Minister Péter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest.

"Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."

Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.

How the downfall of Serbia's Vučiċ mirrored that of Hungary's Orbán

Hungarian MPs scrap Orbán's anti-LGBTQ measures

In the ensuing decades, conservative, Socialist-Liberal, and Fidesz-led governments have all contemplated, but ultimately refused to open the files.

Since 1998, it has been possible to apply for your own file, and for historians to research those of others. But many names were blacked out, and many files withheld by the post-communist secret services for their own use.

Over the past 36 years, there have been frequent leaks of data from the files, as successive governments tried to damage their opponents. Many files were also shredded, as the Communist party lost its grip in 1988-89.

From Wednesday, the names and personal data of around 60,000 people recruited by the communist-era secret services have become available on the nyitottaktak.hu website .

A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer.

Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.

These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided.

Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.

Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary.

Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.

Krisztian Ungváry, a historian who has long campaigned for the full release of the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power.

"In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna Borvendég, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party.

Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

articles.title: In 2009, a Virginia woman paid $7 for a Renoir at a Harpers Ferry flea market; it had been stolen from Baltimore's museum in 1951, and in 2014 a judge sent it back
articles.summary: A Virginia woman unknowingly purchased a stolen Renoir painting for just $7 at a flea market, leading to a federal court case and its return to the Baltimore Museum of Art after 63 years. Discover the extraordinary journey of this artwork and the implications for art ownership rights.
articles.body: A trip to a flea market led to an unusual case of art ownership when a woman from Virginia realised that she had bought a small painting by French Impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir. What was initially something like an inexpensive acquisition at a thrift store became part of a federal lawsuit involving the Baltimore Museum of Art. The painting's path from a West Virginia flea market to a Virginia courtroom raised the question of whether an innocent purchase can establish ownership rights.According to the US Department of Justice, the painting Paysage Bords de Seine had been stolen from the Baltimore Museum of Art in November 1951. Martha Fuqua, a resident of Lovettsville, Virginia, alleged that she bought the painting from a flea market at Harper’s Ferry for only $7 in 2009. The painting came to light when Ms Fuqua tried to auction it in 2012. Museum records and a police report linked the painting to the Baltimore Museum of Art, which asserted ownership under federal law on January 10, 2014.A $7 discovery with an extraordinary history The work, also known as On the Shore of the Seine, was painted by Renoir in 1879. It is a miniature landscape that measures roughly 5.5 by 9 inches and was painted in oil on linen. According to a PRWeb release announcing the museum's exhibition, it was executed on a napkin at one of the restaurants on the riverbank in France. The painting was part of the collection of Saidie A. May of Baltimore, who purchased it from a Paris gallery in 1926.Afterwards, it was loaned to the Baltimore Museum of Art by her in 1937 under the terms of her will, and it belonged to the Museum even after her death. The painting was stolen during an exhibition at the Museum in November 1951. The loss took on special importance once the Museum realised that the documents regarding loans highlighted the connection of the lost artwork with the collection of May.How the theft came to light decades later Fuqua explained that she had seen the painting but was supposedly more interested in its elaborate framing than the actual painting. She found the painting in a box of miscellaneous items at a flea market. It came along with other items such as a doll and a plastic cow; therefore, she had not known the value of the painting at the very beginning, even though it had an identification tag from Renoir.The painting drew attention in September 2012 after Fuqua contacted the Potomack Company, an auction house in Alexandria, Virginia, to sell it. The painting was valued at about $75,000, but the estimates were higher. Before the auction took place, there were some doubts about the painting's ownership history. The Baltimore Museum of Art began researching its archives and found evidence that the painting had been on loan to the museum since May.Later, the theft report made in 1951 was found, which confirmed that the painting had been stolen from the museum. The FBI seized the painting in October 2012, stopping the auction process. Therefore, the Renoir scandal suggests that it is necessary to maintain historical documentation records, especially in situations where artworks are being traded without proper gallery or auction channels.A federal judge settles the ownership disputeThis matter finally came before the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. In the ruling issued on January 10 2014, Judge Leonie Brinkema ordered judgment in favour of the Baltimore Museum of Art as there was enough evidence to prove the ownership of the museum. Fuqua claimed that she was an innocent buyer and was entitled to keep the painting. However, the court stated that even when a purchase is made in good faith, it could not overcome the documented ownership of stolen property.Notably, the judge did not make any pronouncement on the truthfulness of the account of the flea market purchase by her. With the ruling, the museum was poised to reclaim its lost piece of art. The ruling closed a dispute that had gone public in the country and made it clear that just a purchase does not imply ownership. Thus, for the Baltimore Museum of Art, this verdict brought back the painting that was missing for more than sixty years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: Bihar flags 1,700 teachers appointed with fake certificates; verification done for 2.4 lakh of 3.2 lakh, action ordered and salary, attendance reforms reviewed.
articles.body: Patna: The education department has ordered action against around 1,700 teachers who allegedly secured appointments using fake certificates and directed officials to expedite verification of the remaining records, education minister Mithilesh Tiwari said during a review meeting held on Wednesday.The minister said verification of certificates had been completed for 2.40 lakh of the 3.20 lakh teachers whose credentials are under scrutiny. All schools, including Saraswati Vidya Niketan model schools, will be equipped with CCTV cameras.The meeting discussed salary anomalies affecting seven categories of teachers, particularly the denial of pay protection to head teachers. articles.title: Police launch investigation after two inmates die in Nottinghamshire prison
articles.summary: The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed two men died in custody on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Two inmates have died in custody at a prison in Nottinghamshire.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed two men died at HMP Ranby - a Category C training and resettlement prison near Retford - on Wednesday.

Nottinghamshire Police said it was working with the Prison Service to establish the circumstances around the deaths.

A spokesperson for the Prison Service: "As with all deaths in custody, the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman will investigate, and we will respond to its findings in due course."

The Prison Service said it would not be commenting further at this time.

Det Insp James Oakton added: "An investigation has been launched at HMP Ranby following the deaths of two prisoners on Wednesday.

"We are working closely with the prison service to establish the circumstances surrounding these deaths, and a thorough investigation is under way.

"The families of those involved are being supported, and our thoughts are with them at this difficult time."
